title: Miracles
hookLine: Christians differ on how often God acts beyond nature; all see the world itself as a gift

lines: THE GOOD WINE KEPT UNTIL NOW.
cards: "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee." That's how John sums up a wedding. The wine ran out.

Jesus told the servants to fill six stone waterpots with water, and they filled them to the brim. What was carried to the steward of the feast was wine, and the steward said the good wine had been kept until now.

A strange first wonder: no fever cured, no storm stilled, just a party that didn't have to end early. And it opens a question Christians still talk through: how often does God act beyond the ordinary run of things?

teach.b: You met this wedding in year one. Where the King James says miracles, John's Greek says signs. A sign points somewhere.
At Cana, John says, Jesus "manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." The wine pointed at the one who made it. Then the honest disagreement.

teach.h: HOW OFTEN DOES GOD ACT TODAY?
teach.b: Christians differ on how often God acts beyond nature today. In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, people pray boldly for healings and wonders now, and tell of seeing them.
The Catholic Church investigates reported miracles carefully, including when it names saints.
Some Protestants hold that the dramatic sign gifts belonged mainly to the age of the apostles, and that God now works chiefly through ordinary means: scripture, prayer, people, medicine.
Each is a Christian answer, held with conviction. Underneath them all runs a thread. Augustine, preaching on this same wedding, pointed at the vineyards.
The God who turned water into wine at Cana, he said, does it every year, slowly, through rain and root and vine, and people stop marveling only because it happens every season.

The Psalms sound close: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." And in Psalm 139: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." The sky as a sign.
Your own body as a sign. Whatever a Christian believes about Cana-style wonders today, these texts keep pointing at the ordinary world and calling it marvelous. Rain turning into grapes.
A heart that keeps beating while you sleep.

how: Christians differ on miracles today: Pentecostal and charismatic churches pray openly for healings and wonders, the Catholic Church investigates reported miracles (including in naming saints), and some Protestant traditions emphasize God's work through ordinary means.

o: signs: wonders that point past themselves to God
magic tricks that prove a teacher is powerful
lucky breaks with no meaning beyond themselves

p: water into wine at a wedding
the vine does it every year

s: at Cana, Jesus's first sign heals a sick person
it turns water into wine at a wedding, and John calls it the beginning of miracles.
Christians all agree on how often miracles happen today
some pray boldly for wonders now, the Catholic Church investigates reported miracles, and some Protestants hold the sign gifts belonged to the apostles' age.
Augustine pointed at vineyards to talk about Cana
he said the God who made wine at Cana does it every year through the vine.

games.q: you're a servant at the wedding in Cana. the wine is gone, and Jesus tells you to fill the stone waterpots with water. what do you do?
o: fill them to the brim and carry some to the steward.
slip out and buy more wine instead.
games.why: the servants filled them up to the brim. the steward tasted water made wine and said the good wine had been kept until now.

practice: Pick one ordinary thing within reach, your own hand, a glass of water, the light on the wall, and look at it as if nobody had ever shown it to you. Where did it come from, and what had to go right for it to be here?
Stay with it until it starts to feel a little strange, and if you pray, say a plain thank you for it.

wordCard.voice: Miracles. Signs, in John's word: wonders that point past themselves. And for Augustine, the slow wonders of every season too.

orig.note: Greek: a sign — John's word for what the King James calls miracles.

carryVoice: Your line: every day a miracle. A week that began in the dark night ends on wonder. Rest well.
